headline: Naidu's Amaravati offers a model for ambitious, planned urban development
content: This week’s National Interest is datelined Amaravati, the new capital N Chandrababu Naidu is building for Andhra Pradesh, just across the river Krishna from Vijayawada. It isn’t exactly about Amaravati, though. Our central theme is the idea. It’s a novelty in Indian politics, audacious in an era when no politician wants to embark on something she or he cannot complete within one term; or four years, with the fifth reserved for electioneering. Building a Capital takes much longer. One term may not be enough to flaunt it to voters as a success. And what happens if you lose power, as Mr Naidu did in 2019, just after barely collecting his first “pool” of land? His successor, Y S Jagan Mohan Reddy, and his YSRCP (Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party) called the project a sham, intended to benefit one caste, Mr Naidu’s own, since most farmers pooling land for the project were fellow Kamma. Mr Reddy scrapped the project, stopped annuity payments to farmers who had contributed their land, and declared that Andhra Pradesh would have three Capitals instead: Vizag as the executive Capital, Amaravati the legislative Capital and Kurnool the judicial Capital. Decentralisation might be an interesting idea, but not like this. Andhra Pradesh is a large state, and the distance between Vizag and Kurnool is about 700 km, with Amaravati (Vijayawada) exactly in the middle. This deserved to be called Tughlaq-like, which I did. And while Mr Reddy and his party leaders remained polite, Sakshi, the newspaper owned by his family, which had Telugu rights to publish National Interest, dropped it. That, however, is a mere sidelight in a serious discourse. Mr Naidu’s commitment is underlined by the fact that he never abandoned the idea. He promised to revive it and is now building it at warp speed. So fast, indeed, that even if there’s a change of government in the future, there will be little left to reverse. The new Capital is becoming a reality faster than electoral fortunes turn. That persistence with such an ambitious, expansive and expensive idea is what makes this project remarkable. The idea of building a new living, political, commercial, hi-tech, cultural and educational city with a soul is unfamiliar to us. We have built sarkari enclaves out of necessity: Gandhinagar, Naya Raipur, even Bhubaneswar. But these are merely seats of government. The only new city independent India has built is Chandigarh, designed for half a million people. It now has perhaps 1.4 million. That’s no city, even if it’s my hometown for all practical purposes. According to a report submitted by the Indian Institute of Human Settlements (IIHS) to the 15th Finance Commission, all cities built since Independence house no more than, hold your breath, 130 million people. These are mostly glorified colonies for ministers, legislators, officials, employees, their families and domestic workers. There’s no commerce, entrepreneurship or culture. For all that, you go to an old city nearby. Building a city, or even significantly upgrading an existing one, is an idea India has been fundamentally averse to. Why invest resources in cities when, as Gandhi told us, India lives in its villages? Those villages are so rotten in terms of quality of life, so short of opportunity and so socially unequal that millions have been leaving them for cities. Yet planned spending on cities, whether the hundreds we inherited, some dating back millennia, or those that grew chaotically into urban sprawls, was seen as a waste and a political liability. That’s why even existing cities, without exception, have decayed over time. Meanwhile, India urbanised as millions left their villages for these same cities, mostly settling in slums that the mafia gradually came to control. What’s called a slum in Mumbai goes by the name of “unauthorised colonies” in Delhi, which every political party promises to legalise. Residents are condemned to live in the same muck, with open drains. Overhanging wires and cables across the streets make them resemble a rainforest, though one made of plastic. Mumbai has been avidly cannibalising its decrepit old mills and slums. The good thing is that it’s finally building a subcity, Navi Mumbai, with the Trans-Harbour Link connecting the island city to the mainland. It’s a work in progress. Delhi employed the lazier ploy of letting large suburbs come up in Gurugram and Noida, creating a commuting and traffic nightmare as vehicles travel long distances between the three.  A large majority of Delhi’s population, however, continues to live in subhuman conditions in its unauthorised colonies. Sanjay Gandhi gave these settlements a cute name: JJ colonies, or jhuggi-jhopdi (slum and hutment). Many have been partly gentrified over time, with minimal, if any, municipal facilities. Satya Niketan, where a building collapse in September killed seven students, is one such. Bengaluru has expanded haphazardly, with the world’s worst connectivity between its city centre and economic engines. It gets flooded up to the second floor in some of its richest colonies and thirsts for water the rest of the year. The tanker mafia rules India’s Silicon Valley. And what do we say about Kolkata? Barring some new developments on the outskirts, it’s difficult to describe anything there as a slum. Most of its population still lives with a similar quality of life. Just one major Indian city bucked this trend, and it wasn’t yet a metro. Hyderabad woke up to add the muscle of tech entrepreneurship to its soul and historic spirit. It was Mr Naidu who started this during his first of four chief ministerships, beginning in 1995. He founded Cyberabad to compete with Bengaluru. His successor, Y S Rajasekhara Reddy of the Congress, carried that Telugu entrepreneurship forward, and built on it. The city didn’t just survive political change, it thrived.Mr Naidu was told by many, including much of our ‘old school’ socialist commentariat, that he had erred by focusing on the city, playing chief executive officer of the state and ignoring the poor in the process. His persistence with Amaravati, despite the 2019 electoral setback, is now seen as evidence that he’s incorrigible. And it’s a good thing. To repeat, this column isn’t about Amaravati. That deserves a full episode of “Writings On The Wall” sometime later. But a few points, especially its innovation in urbanisation, deserve mention. The biggest challenge to building infrastructure in our country is land acquisition. How come there were minimal protests in Amaravati? Mr Naidu’s first innovation was his land-pooling scheme. Farmers were invited to pool their land instead of selling it. For every acre, he committed to returning a share in developed residential and commercial plots. And what would farmers do until the Capital was built and the land monetised? Mr Naidu promised an annuity, starting at ₹50,000 per acre annually, with a 5 per cent increase every year. Today it is ₹95,000, far more than what any farmer earns from an acre. About 33,000 acres were pooled this way. The government added another 20,000 acres of its own around the planned city, taking its total area to about 53,000 acres or 217.23 square km. It’s a planned city, with grids neatly dividing it into blocks of 1 square km. Best of all, the entire government — offices, ministers, legislators, the High Court, the Vidhan Sabha and the Legislative Council, and employees of all classes — will be housed along a 7-km-long central median, occupying just 7 square km. The rest will be developed privately, with universities, tech hubs and an IBM Quantum Hub (120-qubit to begin with), scheduled for inauguration next February. This is important because governments usually consume every vacant piece of land available. Here, the government owns no more than these 7 square km. This is the second innovation. The third is a kind of political insurance. What if someone invests on the strength of your promised incentives and you lose power? Mr Naidu passed a law this week to protect investment and ensure that a share of the taxes received from these entrepreneurs went into escrow accounts, with mandatory payouts on committed dates. It’s around these political and administrative innovations that he is building this trillion-rupee city. It’s a good example for other chief ministers. Take some risks and, as he says, create wealth so the government can earn more and distribute it. By special arrangement with ThePrint

headline: Tejashwi accuses BJP MLA Maithili Thakur’s father of land grabbing
content: PATNA Leader of Opposition in Bihar Legislative Assembly Tejashwi Yadav on Friday (November 13, 2026) accused BJP MLA Maithili Thakur’s father Ramesh Thakur of forcefully encroaching private and government land. The villagers of Pokharbhinda panchayat in Darbhanga district has alleged Mr. Ramesh Thakur of encroaching on a government road and privately owned land while fencing the plot. The Deputy Collector Land Reforms (DCLR) Ajya Kumar went to the encroachment area on November 12, 2026, conducted a land survey, and then removed the illegal construction at the site. One complainant, Gagan Kumar Mishra, has written to Circle Officer (CO) on September 7, 2026, alleging Mr. Thakur of encroaching the land. “BJP MLA Maithili Thakur and her father, Ramesh Thakur, have illegally occupied government land worth hundreds of crores—along with public roads, communal ritual sites, and private plots—in the Tardih block of Darbhanga district,”Mr. Yadav wrote in social media post on X. He further said, “The administration has confirmed the authenticity of these encroachments. It is ironic, the very MLA who claimed to see a “Jungle Raj” (lawlessness) is now, under this so-called “Mangal Raj” (good governance), seizing both government and villagers’ land.” A day earlier, Ms. Thakur, who represents the Alinagar Assembly constituency, denied the charges saying that her family has valid land document. She has not reacted after the removal of the encroachment. Hitting out at Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, Mr. Yadav said when a Chief Minister with criminal tendencies provides protection, his MLAs and Ministers become emboldened to commit crimes. “Targeting ordinary citizens, they have accelerated their activities by seizing government land, orchestrating the murders of government officials, engaging in corruption and moral misconduct, and intensifying extortion, robbery, and dacoity,” Mr. Yadav alleged. He also mentioned that there is no government in Bihar and tt is the NDA’s own MLAs who are now troubling the public. He further alleged that corruption and crime have crossed all limits. He asked what do Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah have to say about the “crimes and immoral acts recently committed by NDA MLAs”. He also named several other MLAs of the ruling coalition, alleging that an NDA MLA from Chirag Paswan’s Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) party, representing Belsand Assembly constituency, Amit Kumar, has seized land worth several hundred crores across the Muzaffarpur and Sitamarhi districts. “Another NDA MLA from the LJP (RV) has been implicated in the murder of the Executive Officer (EO) of the Dehri-Dalmianagar Municipal Council in Rohtas district. According to the official’s wife, the LJP (RV) MLA had her husband killed because he refused to pay a commission,” Mr. Yadav said. Executive Officer (EO) of Dalmianagar Municipal Council, Vimal Kumar, was beaten to death in Bihar’s Aurangabad district late on August 1, 2026). His wife Babita Kumari had accused Rajiv Ranjan Sing alias Sonu Singh, LJP (RV) MLA of Dehri-on-Sone, of being behind his murder. Mr. Yadav’s brother Tej Pratap Yadav has also slammed Mr. Thakur saying that illegal occupation of the land of the poor and farmers will not be tolerated at any cost. “The allegations emerging against Ramesh Thakur, the father of MLA Maithili Thakur, of land grabbing and threatening people are deeply troubling. These allegations must be investigated impartially at a high leve, “ Mr. Tej Pratap, the National President of Janshakti Janata Dal, wrote on X.
